nodes.content: Develop unsupervised speech recognition accent adaptation that separates pronunciation shifts from speaker and channel variation without sacrificing existing accents.
requirements: Reduce unseen-accent word error rate ≥15% relative to frozen recognizer using only unlabeled adaptation speech.
Limit existing-accent WER increases to one percentage point under independently varying speakers and channels.

nodes.content: Train pronunciation LoRA on confidence-filtered pseudo-transcripts with speaker/channel adversaries; gate adaptation by accent prototypes, retaining frozen decoding otherwise.
Can accent-prototype distances trigger pronunciation LoRA without false activations under independently changed speakers and microphones?
Speaker/channel-invariant accent prototypes will gate LoRA for ≥80% of unseen-accent utterances but ≤5% of existing-accent utterances.
Train adversarial accent prototypes on unlabeled speech; calibrate the gate on existing accents; measure activation and WER across crossed speakers/channels.
Train adversarial prototypes on unlabeled speech; test unseen/existing accent gate activation across 12 speakers crossed with four microphones.
Across 12 speakers and four microphones, prototype gating activated on 84% unseen-accent and 3.8% existing-accent utterances.
Retain adversarial prototype gating for LoRA evaluation: unseen-accent activation exceeds 80% while existing-accent activation remains below 5%.
Fit gated pronunciation LoRA using unlabeled speech; compare frozen/adapted WER on unseen and existing accents across held-out speaker–microphone crosses.
AccentGate-WER v1: gated LoRA checkpoint and frozen-versus-adapted WER tables stratified by accent, held-out speaker, and microphone.
Bootstrap AccentGate-WER v1 tables across held-out speaker–microphone crosses; check ≥15% unseen-accent WER reduction and ≤1-point existing-accent increase.
Bootstrapped paired WER shows 6.3% of existing-accent utterances worsened; frozen fallback implies gate activation exceeded 5%.
Worst-case speaker–microphone calibration with augmentation-consistent gating will yield ≥80% unseen-accent and ≤5% existing-accent activation on held-out crosses.
Following n10's 6.3% regressions, recalibrate worst-case gate thresholds on unlabeled existing-accent speech; test augmentation-consistent activation across held-out crosses.
Infer accent-specific phoneme substitution transducers from unlabeled ASR lattices using speaker/channel-invariant embeddings; conservatively rerank frozen beams.
Mine unlabeled lattice confusions, fit accent transducers, confidence-gate frozen-beam reranking, and assess unseen/existing WER across speaker/channel crosses.
Reuse AccentGate-WER v1's speaker–microphone strata to partition unlabeled speech; mine lattice confusions and fit accent-specific phoneme transducers.
LatticeShift v1: accent-specific phoneme transducer weights, confidence-gated beam-reranking code, and speaker–microphone-stratified unlabeled lattice counts.
Do LatticeShift v1's learned phoneme substitutions transfer across independently varied speakers and microphones without tracking channel artifacts?
Unlike microphone-specific substitutions, LatticeShift's accent substitutions will cut unseen-accent WER ≥15% across held-out speaker–microphone crosses.
Run LatticeShift v1 and microphone-specific transducer controls on held-out speaker–microphone crosses; compare unseen-accent WER reductions and existing-accent changes.
On held-out crosses, LatticeShift reduced unseen-accent WER 18% versus frozen; microphone-specific transducers achieved 6%, with existing-accent WER +0.4 points.
Prefer LatticeShift reranking over prototype-gated LoRA: 18% unseen-accent WER reduction, +0.4-point existing-accent change, versus gating regressions.
Compare gated LoRA, LatticeShift v1, and frozen decoding across held-out speaker–microphone crosses; report unseen-accent WER reduction and existing-accent drift.
Recalibrated gating activated on 82% unseen-accent and 4.2% existing-accent utterances; LatticeShift cut WER 18% versus LoRA’s 12%.
How many unlabeled adaptation hours does LatticeShift need for reliable phoneme substitutions across held-out speaker–microphone pairs?
Subsample LatticeShift adaptation audio to 0.5/2/8 hours; assess held-out WER against n19's 18% gain to identify minimum viable duration.
Adapt phoneme-posterior normalization using speaker/channel augmentation consistency, while anchoring frozen predictions on unlabeled existing-accent speech.
Augmentation-consistent posterior normalization with frozen-prediction anchoring will reduce unseen-accent WER ≥15% while limiting existing-accent drift to ≤1 point.
Train posterior normalization with speaker/microphone augmentations and frozen-prediction anchoring; measure unseen and existing accent WER on held-out crosses.
Posterior normalization reduced unseen-accent WER 9% versus frozen, below 15% required, despite +0.3-point existing-accent drift.
Does frozen-prediction anchoring suppress adaptation of accent-specific vowel mergers, limiting unseen-accent WER reduction to 9%?
Relaxing frozen-prediction anchoring for vowel-merger phonemes will lower merger-word WER ≥5% relative to anchored normalization.
Ablate vowel-merger anchoring in posterior normalization; compare merger-word and existing-accent WER against fully anchored decoding across held-out crosses.
Relaxed vowel anchoring cut merger-word WER 7% versus anchored; unseen-accent WER improved 16% versus frozen, existing-accent drift +0.7 points.
Can unlabeled lattice statistics identify vowel-merger phonemes for anchor relaxation without exceeding one-point existing-accent WER drift?
Mine unlabeled cross-speaker/microphone lattice confusions to select relaxed vowels; compare WER against anchored and vowel-relaxed baselines on held-out crosses.
Lattice-selected vowels cut unseen-accent WER 15.6% versus frozen, with +0.6-point existing-accent drift on held-out speaker–microphone crosses.
Choose lattice-selected vowel relaxation over fixed anchoring and preselected mergers: 15.6% unseen-accent WER reduction, +0.6-point existing-accent drift.
Build speaker/channel-invariant, pseudo-labeled phonetic exemplar memory from unlabeled augmentations; acoustically rescore frozen hypotheses with conservative fallback.
Build augmentation-invariant phonetic exemplars, rescore frozen beams with confidence-gated retrieval, then test WER across held-out speaker–microphone crosses.
Use LatticeShift v1's lattice counts to select stable pseudo-phoneme segments; train augmentation-invariant exemplar embeddings and a confidence-gated beam rescorer.
ExemplarRescore v1: unlabeled phonetic embedding index, gated frozen-beam rescorer, and speaker–microphone-stratified pseudo-phoneme provenance logs.
Evaluate ExemplarRescore v1 against frozen and LatticeShift decoding on held-out speaker–microphone crosses; report accent WER and false retrieval rates.
ExemplarRescore cut unseen-accent WER 17% versus frozen, with +0.5-point existing-accent drift; LatticeShift achieved 18% and +0.4 points.
Select LatticeShift as primary: 18% unseen-accent WER reduction and +0.4-point existing-accent drift outperform exemplar and lattice-selected normalization.
